messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Vinh

Vinh was fifty-one when his wife left him in the emergency room with a fractured wrist and a story he could barely piece together. It had happened on a Tuesday evening in their Arlington home—an argument about money, about his long hours at the tax office, about something so ordinary he could no longer retrieve the exact words. What remained were fragments: the sound of breaking glass, the feeling of being pushed backward into the kitchen counter, his partner's face transformed by rage into something he no longer recognized. Then a blur—his arm bent at an angle that didn't belong, the drive to the hospital, and the slow understanding that the person he'd chosen to build a life with had done this to him.

The wrist healed. The bruises faded. But something in Vinh's nervous system had been rewired that night, and he had spent the past eighteen months learning to live in a state of constant vigilance. His wife had moved out after two weeks of tense silence, and he'd remained in the house—the same house where it happened—unable to leave it and unable to feel safe inside it.

Exhaustion had become his constant companion. The long days at the tax office, where he reviewed financial records with the same meticulous attention he'd always brought to the work, now drained him in ways he couldn't explain. By mid-afternoon, his body would feel heavy, his mind sluggish, and in that state of fatigue something terrible would happen: his thoughts would spiral into worst-case scenarios, or a sudden fragment of that night would surface—the specific angle of light through the kitchen window, the smell of his own fear—and he would become convinced that danger was imminent. When he was tired, he couldn't trust his own judgment about what was safe. A colleague approaching his desk to ask about a file would trigger an acute startle response; his heart would race as if the threat were real and present. Unpredictable moments—a phone call from an unknown number, an unexpected knock at his office door—would send him into a state of heightened alert that felt indistinguishable from the minutes before the violence itself.

These triggers fed directly into a pervasive sense of threat that had come to dominate his waking hours. Vinh had rearranged his home office so that his desk faced the doorway and his back was always against the wall—a position that felt essential, though he couldn't fully articulate why. When he was in other people's homes or in public spaces, he felt a gnawing anxiety unless he could position himself with a clear view of exits and approaching figures. He found himself constantly checking behind him in hallways at work, a habit so ingrained now that he barely noticed he was doing it. The threat felt constant and shapeless, not tied to any specific danger but rather to a fundamental conviction that something terrible could happen at any moment, that his body and mind were not safe even when objectively nothing was wrong.

The fragments of memory that intruded without warning intensified this sense of threat. A particular smell—cologne mixed with sweat—would cause a piece of the evening to surface: not the whole narrative, but a sensory flash that felt as immediate and dangerous as the original moment. There were gaps in what he could remember, entire stretches of time that had simply vanished from his mind, and the incompleteness of the memory somehow made it worse. The uncontrolled intrusions meant he could be sitting in a client meeting, and suddenly he would feel the phantom sensation of his arm being twisted, or hear the sound of his own voice saying something he couldn't quite recover. These involuntary memories would then trigger the threat response all over again—his heart rate climbing, his muscles tensing, his eyes scanning the room for danger.

What frightened Vinh most, though, was what he had come to believe about his future. Nothing good could happen to him anymore—this conviction had settled into his bones like a chronic illness. The betrayal by someone he'd loved and trusted had shattered something fundamental in how he understood the world. He felt hollowed out, as though the violence had transformed him into something less than human, an object that could be broken and discarded. These dark beliefs about himself and his prospects fed the threat monitoring, made every trigger feel more dangerous, made the intrusive memories feel more predictive of what was to come. He had begun to avoid situations where he felt unprepared or out of control, which meant he was avoiding more and more of his life. His colleagues had noticed his withdrawal; his supervisor had gently asked if everything was alright. He'd made excuses about the divorce, about needing time.

What finally brought Vinh to seek help was a panic attack at work three weeks ago—a full-body conviction that he was in mortal danger while sitting alone in his office on a quiet afternoon. He'd sat in his car in the parking garage for two hours afterward, unable to drive, unable to move. That night, he'd called a therapist. He was terrified that he was losing his mind, but underneath that terror was something quieter and more desperate: a faint hope that someone might help him understand why the person he'd loved had hurt him, and whether he would ever feel safe again.
